h1: Cleaning and reusing old beer bottles for your homebrew
title: Cleaning and Reusing Old Beer Bottles | Craft Beer School
desc: How to strip labels, clean crusted bottles and sanitise them for homebrew, plus which bottles to bin and how to store them clean.
teaser: A bottle that looks clean can still be hiding a ring of yeast at the shoulder. Here is the routine that gets it every time.
standfirst: Reused bottles are free and plentiful in India, but each one carries someone else's history. Here is a simple routine to clean, inspect and sanitise them so your beer tastes of your brewing and nothing else.
sections:
The best cleaning happens the minute a bottle is empty. Rinse it three times with warm water, shaking hard. Then stand it upside down to drain. Dried yeast and beer residue take seconds to remove when wet and hours when crusted.

If you collect bottles from friends or a scrap dealer, they will not have done this. Expect to deal with dried sediment, cigarette ends, the occasional insect and, in the monsoon, mould.
Cleaning and sanitising are two jobs

Cleaning removes dirt you can see. Sanitising kills the microbes you cannot. Sanitiser does not work on a dirty surface, because the residue protects whatever lives underneath. So every bottle is cleaned first and sanitised just before filling. Our guide to cleaning vs sanitising explains the difference in detail.

Oxygen-based cleaners do most of the work for you. Look for a brewing cleaner such as PBW or an unscented sodium percarbonate cleaner.

  1. Fill a bucket with warm water, around 40 to 50 °C. Dissolve the cleaner at the dose on the pack.
  2. Submerge the bottles, filling each one. Leave them overnight.
  3. Most paper labels slide off by morning. Foil and plastic labels may need a scraper.
  4. Scrub the inside with a bottle brush, paying attention to the shoulder.
  5. Rinse thoroughly with clean water, at least twice.

Avoid scented household detergents. They leave a film and a perfume that ruins head retention and aroma. Avoid bleach too unless you rinse it out completely, because chlorine reacts with compounds in beer to give a medicinal, plasticky flavour.

Hold each bottle up to a bright light or a window and look down the neck. You are looking for:

  • A ring or film at the shoulder or bottom.
  • Dark specks or fuzz, which mean mould.
  • Chips on the lip or cracks in the glass.

Pay extra attention to bottles from a scrap dealer or a party. People put all sorts into empty bottles. A bottle that held anything other than beer, especially oil, paint thinner or a chemical, should not come back into your brewing.

Chipped or cracked bottles go straight to recycling. Bottles with stubborn film get another soak and scrub. If mould will not come out after two rounds, recycle the bottle. A bottle costs very little. A batch lost to infection costs a month.

On bottling day, sanitise the clean bottles. A no-rinse acid sanitiser such as Star San, mixed with water at the dose on the bottle, needs about a minute of contact. Fill each bottle a quarter full, shake, pour back and drain upside down. Do not worry about the foam left inside. It will not harm the beer.

Iodophor works well too and also needs no rinse at the correct dilution. If your tap water is hard, mixing sanitiser with filtered or RO water keeps it effective for longer.

Some brewers sterilise bottles in an oven. It works, but glass that is heated or cooled unevenly can crack. It also takes time. Chemical sanitiser is quicker and safer for most people.

Once clean and dry, store bottles upside down in a crate or capped with a square of foil over the neck. That keeps dust and insects out. In humid months, make sure they are fully dry before you cover them, or you will grow something inside. Sanitise again just before use regardless.

On bottling day itself, set up in order: sanitiser bucket, bottle tree, filling station, capper. Keep caps in a small bowl of sanitiser so you are not reaching into a dry bag with wet hands. Fill, cap and move on, so no sanitised bottle sits open for long. A tidy line halves the time and the chance of a mistake.

A bottle tree, a stand that holds bottles upside down to drain, speeds up drying and is worth having if you bottle often.

If one bottle in a batch tastes sour, gushes or smells off while the rest are fine, the bottle is usually to blame. If the whole batch is off, look further upstream at your fermenter, tubing or bottling bucket. Our list of first homebrew mistakes covers the usual suspects.

Bottle hygiene is the easiest part of brewing to get right and one of the easiest to skip. The harder part is knowing where else contamination hides in your process and how to design a routine that keeps the whole system clean, not just the glass.
faqs: What is the easiest way to remove beer labels?
Soak the bottles overnight in warm water with an oxygen-based cleaner. Most paper labels slide off in the morning.
Can I use dishwashing liquid to clean bottles?
It is best avoided. Scented detergents leave a film and a smell that damage head retention and aroma.
Do I need to rinse Star San out of bottles?
No. At the correct dilution it is a no-rinse sanitiser and the leftover foam does not harm the beer.
